# Character Consistency

## Purpose

Define one canonical identity per character and make sure no two characters
can be mistaken for each other. Identity lives in `character.yaml` as fixed
descriptors, a list of distinguishing features, and a record of which cast
members the character could be confused with. An image model does not know
who anyone is. It draws from descriptions and reference images, and when two
of those are close it merges them, whatever the caption calls the result.

## Use When

- Creating or revising a character bible entry.
- A new character joins a cast that already has someone of similar age,
  build, or clothing.
- A review records an `identity` finding: a character drawn with another's
  face, or two versions of one person in a panel.
- Wardrobe changes mid-story and the change needs a named state.

## Inputs

- Facts about the character from `production/story/story-bible.yaml`, with
  the source's quoted descriptions.
- `production/characters/<CHAR_ID>/character.yaml` and `wardrobe.yaml` if
  present.
- Every other character file in the cast, for the comparison in step 4.
- Approved sheets registered in `production/references/manifest.yaml`.
- `production/project.yaml` for `color_mode`.

## Process

1. Assign the ID (`CHAR_<NAME>`) and fill `description`: `summary`, `age`,
   `build`, `hair`, `face`, `skin`. Describe shapes. "Long face, deep-set
   eyes, broken nose" can be drawn and checked; "weathered good looks"
   cannot.
2. Write `distinguishing_features`: the things that separate this character
   from everyone else in the cast. One is required; aim for three. At least
   one sits above the neck so a close-up still identifies them, and at least
   one shows in silhouette. Each has to survive the comic's `color_mode`:
   in monochrome, "red hair" distinguishes nobody, while "light cropped
   hair" against "dark hood" does.
3. Freeze the phrasing. Each trait has one wording, reused everywhere.
   `prompt_summary` is a single sentence built from those wordings, and the
   compiler uses it verbatim. A synonym in one prompt is a different
   character in one render.
4. Compare the character with every other one they share a page with. Two
   characters of similar age, build, hair, or dress are visually adjacent:
   list each in the other's `visually_adjacent_to`. Prompts state the
   difference for every adjacent pair that appears together.
5. Separate adjacent characters by design. Give them different face shapes,
   hair, facial hair, builds, and clothing silhouettes, and change the
   design until at least three of those five differ. If Mara's deckhand is
   also grey and wiry in a dark coat, he gets a beard, a round face, and a
   short jacket. Changing a name changes nothing.
6. Run the silhouette test. Filled in solid black, each character in a scene
   should still be identifiable by outline: coat length, hood, hair mass,
   posture, height.
7. Pin every sided feature. A torn left cuff, a cut on the left hand, a scar
   over the right eye: write the side in the feature itself, since image
   models mirror freely.
8. Define wardrobe states in `wardrobe.yaml` as outfits with an `id`
   (`WARD_<CHARACTER>_<NAME>`), `description`, `layers`, `accessories`,
   `hands`, and `used_in`. A coat that is intact in one issue and torn in
   the next is two outfits. Blood, soaking, and injuries are state tags in
   the panel ledger and do not belong here. Set `default_wardrobe`.
9. Give recurring secondary characters the same treatment at smaller scale:
   a character file, distinguishing features, an adjacency check.
   Substitutions happen most often to the people nobody designed.
10. Version changes. An approved identity is never edited in place; a real
    change (aging, disfigurement, a user change) produces new sheets with
    the next `_V##`, and the old assets become `superseded`.
11. Cross-check after every change: `character.yaml`, `wardrobe.yaml`, and
    the approved sheets must agree. When an approved sheet shows something
    the text lacks, update the text to match the image.

## Outputs

- `production/characters/<CHAR_ID>/character.yaml` (`character` schema).
- `production/characters/<CHAR_ID>/wardrobe.yaml` (`wardrobe` schema).
- A sheet plan for `character-sheet-generation`: which sheets each
  character needs.

## Quality Bar

- Every character has at least one distinguishing feature above the neck
  and one visible in silhouette.
- No distinguishing feature depends on a color the `color_mode` cannot show.
- `visually_adjacent_to` is symmetric: if A lists B, B lists A.
- Every adjacent pair differs in at least three of face shape, hair, facial
  hair, build, and clothing silhouette.
- One phrasing per trait, identical wherever it appears.
- Every sided feature names its side.
- Every outfit worn in a page's ledger exists in `wardrobe.yaml`.

## Common Failure Modes

- Trusting names. Two men with short dark hair and dark jackets come back
  as the same man twice, each correctly labeled.
- The model's default face. Left without anchors, every adult of one type
  gets the same generic features.
- Hair or eye color as the only difference in a black-and-white comic.
- Features too small for a panel: eye color, a thin scar, a ring. They pass
  on the sheet and vanish on the page.
- Paraphrased descriptors ("grey cropped hair" in the bible, "short silver
  hair" in a note that reaches a prompt).
- Unsided features that flip between panels.
- Age drift: a boy of twelve drawn as a teenager on one page and a small
  adult on the next, because only "boy" was written down.
- Wardrobe described in prose and never given an ID, so the ledger cannot
  track it.
- A style change that redraws identity anchors along with the line.

## Notes

This skill writes the contract. `character-sheet-generation` draws it,
`reference-selection` attaches it to each page, and `pixel-review` checks
the result. The rule is `rules/visual/character-consistency.md`. Written
description never outranks an approved sheet.
